hints: Look first at the left column. Is the plant cell wall fully permeable or partially permeable, and which living layer actually controls osmosis?
Remember that a concentrated sucrose solution has a very negative water potential. Which way will water move by osmosis, and does water ever stop moving completely in both directions?
walkthrough:
**Identify the partially permeable layer**

Think about what each layer lets through. The cell wall is fully permeable to water and solutes, it is just support.

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane plus tonoplast around the vacuole) is the partially permeable barrier for osmosis. So A and B are right on this column, C and D are wrong.

**Compare water potentials at the start**

Concentrated sucrose solution has lots of solute, so it has a low (more negative) water potential.

The cell contents are more dilute than that solution, so they have a higher (less negative) water potential. Water always moves from higher to lower water potential, so B and D are right here.

**Describe the movement of water correctly**

Osmosis is a two-way movement. Water molecules cross the membrane in both directions all the time.

Because the cell has the higher water potential, there is a net loss: more water moves out than moves in. The cell plasmolyses. That matches B exactly, not a one-way flow with no entry.

options.A: Membrane is correct, but both other statements are wrong. Cell contents have higher, not lower, water potential than concentrated sucrose, and water moves both ways with net loss, not only out.
options.B: All three parts are correct. Membrane is partially permeable, cell has higher water potential than the concentrated solution, so net movement is out with more leaving than entering.
options.C: Cell wall is fully permeable, not partially permeable, and cell contents have higher, not lower, water potential than the concentrated solution.
options.D: Cell wall is wrong as it is fully permeable, and water never moves only one way. There is always movement both ways with a net outflow here.
